evidence.label: Lipschitz Equivalent Separable Banach Spaces Need Not Be Linearly Isomorphic
Bi-Lipschitz Absorption of c0 Without a Linear Copy of c0

headline: Two separable Banach spaces match distances up to fixed factors but are not linearly the same, answering Kalton.
scope: Separable real Banach spaces: one bi-Lipschitz but nonisomorphic pair, and one space that absorbs c₀ bi-Lipschitzly with no linear copy of c₀.
plain: A bi-Lipschitz map stretches or shrinks every distance by at most fixed factors, but need not respect addition. A long-standing question asked whether such a map between two separable Banach spaces forces them to be linearly the same. The first paper proves the answer is no, with explicit factors 4/21 and 76/25, and Lean checks it. The second paper proves a related result: a space that swallows c₀ nonlinearly but contains no linear copy of it. Lean checks that too.
doesNot: This does not give complex-scalar or reflexive examples, and it does not say the space Y lacks an ordinary copy of c₀.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Israel Aharoni and Joram Lindenstrauss, nonseparable examples and the question for separable spaces
scorecard.significanceWhy: It answers two problems from Kalton's 2008 survey that had stayed open for separable Banach spaces.

explanation:
Take the map f(x) = x + sin(x)/2 on the real line. Its slope always lies between 1/2 and 3/2. So f never shrinks a distance below half, or stretches it beyond one and a half times. It sends 0 to 0 and π to π. But it sends π/2 to about 2.071, not to π/2 ≈ 1.571. So f is not linear, yet it controls every distance. A map like this, onto and with two-sided distance bounds, is called bi-Lipschitz.

A Banach space is a vector space with a length for each vector, where good sequences always have limits. It is separable if a countable set comes arbitrarily close to every point. Two Banach spaces are linearly isomorphic if a linear map matches them with bounded distortion. Every linear isomorphism is bi-Lipschitz. The question is the reverse. If a bi-Lipschitz map exists, must a linear isomorphism exist too?

Aharoni and Lindenstrauss built nonseparable counterexamples and asked for separable ones[1]. Ribe later built separable spaces that are uniformly homeomorphic but not isomorphic[2]. That is a weaker kind of matching, with no fixed distance factors. Godefroy, Kalton and Lancien proved a rigidity result. Any Banach space bi-Lipschitz equivalent to c₀ is linearly isomorphic to c₀[3]. Here c₀ is the space of sequences that tend to zero, measured by their largest entry. In the wider quasi-Banach setting, Albiac and Kalton found separable counterexamples for every 0 < p < 1[4]. Kalton listed the separable question as Problem 3 in his 2008 survey[5].

The first paper answers the question negatively for separable Banach spaces[6]. It builds spaces X and Y and a bijection between them. Every distance changes by a factor between 4/21 and 76/25. In decimals that is between about 0.190 and 3.04. Two points 10 apart in X land between about 1.905 and 30.4 apart in Y. Yet X contains a copy of c₀(ℓ₂), a c₀ of Hilbert spaces, while Y contains none[7]. The paper notes this does not rule out an ordinary c₀ inside Y[8]. It also gives no complex-scalar or reflexive version[9].

The obstacle is that a bi-Lipschitz map ignores addition, yet the conclusion is linear. The paper bridges this with Lipschitz-free spaces. These turn a distance-preserving picture into a linear one. A careful geometric condition makes a key linear map completely continuous. Such a map sends every weakly null sequence to a norm-null one[10]. That property blocks any copy of c₀(ℓ₂) in Y.

The second paper treats Kalton's Problem 2[11]. It builds a separable space Z with no linear copy of c₀. Yet Z is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to Z combined with an extra copy of c₀[12]. So Z contains c₀ in the bi-Lipschitz sense, but not linearly. Aharoni proved that every separable metric space embeds bi-Lipschitzly into c₀[13]. So the same Z contains a bi-Lipschitz copy of every separable metric space[14].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, proves both main results. It covers the pair X and Y with the bounds 4/21 and 76/25, and the missing copy of c₀(ℓ₂). It also covers the space Z that absorbs c₀ without a linear copy. No specialist review has been published, but both statements have Lean proofs.
hypeCheck: Major. Both main theorems have Lean proofs; they answer two of Kalton's 2008 problems for separable real Banach spaces.

glossary.meaning: A vector space with a notion of length in which every Cauchy sequence has a limit.
Having a countable set of points that comes arbitrarily close to every point.
A map that changes every distance by a factor between two fixed positive numbers.
Matched by a linear map that is bounded with a bounded inverse.
The space of real sequences that tend to zero, with length given by the largest entry.
Sequences of vectors from the Hilbert space ℓ₂ whose lengths tend to zero.
A Banach space built from a metric space so that Lipschitz maps become linear maps.
A linear map that turns every weakly null sequence into a sequence whose lengths tend to zero.
